cross_cutting: Interface quality is now a design task, not a by-product. Skills such as "impeccable" and "frontend-design" and a Claude Design round trip (import a visual language, or restyle and export) are the quickest ways to remove generic AI styling. Students who did this will share their workflow.
Decide the minimum information a first-time user needs on screen; move everything else behind toggles. This came up for the stair tool, the shading tool and the massing tools alike.

Floor-plan generation is the common weak spot. For early-phase tools, areas, unit blocks and adjacencies are enough; furniture and room layouts can be dropped. Where plans matter, controllable methods exist (rule sets per room, graph-based generation, preference loops with agents).

Choose the format deliberately: web page, Rhino plugin, web page with Rhino in the background, or Rhino Compute for users without Rhino. Each student should state who the user is and pick accordingly.

Several tools point toward the same next question: regulation as a collective, district-scale form rather than a single-lot check (massing envelopes, permeability, view cones, SRO policy). Changing one parameter at district level and quantifying the result is the direction of most interest for Phase 2.
Housekeeping as tools grow: split large HTML files, load 3D context by region, ask Claude in a fresh session to remove unused files, and apply for a GitHub education account if limits are hit.
The pin-up format worked and will be repeated in Phase 2. Peer reviews go to GitHub issues (or the class deck's speaker notes); the recording is processed into these notes so comments are tracked.
